title: Why fixing India's air pollution crisis requires more than technical solutions
where: Explained page, 'Expert Explains' (Shahzad Gani, Centre for Atmospheric Sciences, IIT Delhi)
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; vulnerable sections · GS4 › Environmental ethics; probity in use of public funds
summary: An IIT Delhi atmospheric scientist argues that India knows the sources of its air pollution and must act on them through transport, clean cooking, waste management and regulation, rather than wait for more data or chase technological spectacles.
evolution: Punjab farm fires concentrated in Tarn Taran and Amritsar.
Clean air needs targets, timelines, accountability; NCAP 2.0 being drafted.
Acting before the air turns severe.
Expert view: sources known, act now; look beyond technical fixes.
ideas: A year-round, all-India problem: air pollution is not just Delhi-NCR in winter; transport, household fuels, waste burning, industry and construction pollute all year, while weather only disperses or traps emissions.
GS3 · Pollution
Treating air pollution as a seasonal Delhi issue misses its year-round, nationwide sources.

Sources are known, so act: reducing pollution needs two things, fewer emission sources and cleaner remaining ones; public transport, clean cooking and heating, alternatives to stubble burning, working waste management and industrial regulation.
GS3 · Pollution control / GS2 · Policy
Research should refine interventions, not become a prerequisite for action.
Beyond technical fixes: stubble burning needs an understanding of farmers' economic constraints; firecracker pollution needs changes in social attitudes and community action, not only bans.
GS3 · Agriculture / GS1 · Society
Stubble and firecrackers are social and economic problems, not merely technical ones.

Measure what people breathe: rooftop monitors miss indoor exposure from solid-fuel cooking, which falls mostly on women; street vendors, construction and sanitation workers, and farmers face the highest exposure.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections / GS1 · Women
Exposure, not ambient readings alone, should guide policy so that the most vulnerable are protected.

Spectacle vs substance: smog towers and artificial rain offer the optics of action despite doubts over effectiveness; institutional fixes such as transport, waste and clean energy need sustained funding, coordination and confronting vested interests.
GS3 · Governance of environment / GS4 · Probity
Public money should fund what cuts emissions, not what looks like action.
keywords: Judging success by what people actually breathe, indoors and outdoors
An exposure-centred clean air policy would cover kitchens and workplaces, not just rooftop monitors.
Belief that a gadget can fix a complex social problem
Smog towers reflect techno-solutionism: visible, costly and of doubtful effect.
Visible measures that signal effort without reducing harm
Spectacular projects can give governments the optics of action without cutting emissions.
Fair sharing of environmental burdens and protection
Those with the least choice, such as street vendors and women cooking on solid fuels, bear the most exposure: an environmental justice gap.
Valuing economists, social scientists and practitioners alongside scientists
Clean air needs plural expertise, from agricultural economists to community workers.
examples: Smog towers and artificial rain
spectacle over substance in pollution control
GS4
GS3 · Pollution · GS4 · Probity
Smog towers and artificial rain: the optics of action without real emission cuts.
Rooftop monitor vs smoky kitchen
ambient readings miss indoor exposure
GS3 · Pollution · GS1 · Women
A rooftop monitor cannot see a smoky kitchen: indoor exposure falls mostly on women.
Street vendors and sanitation workers
highest exposure, least choice
GS4
GS2 · Vulnerable sections · GS4 · Environmental justice
Street vendors and sanitation workers: highest exposure, least choice.
pyqs: Key features of the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP).
WHO's revised Air Quality Guidelines and changes needed in NCAP.
Photochemical smog: formation, effects, mitigation; Gothenburg Protocol.
Why air pollution is worse in Delhi than in Mumbai and Kolkata.
Challenges to solid waste management; policy framework.
National Urban Transport Policy: 'moving people' not 'moving vehicles'.

trend.t: Air pollution questions began with geography (why Delhi is worse, 2015), moved to policy (NCAP features 2020, WHO guidelines and NCAP changes 2021) and science (photochemical smog 2022). Related sources are asked separately: urban transport (2014) and solid waste management (2026).
trend.watch: Air quality was asked three years in a row (2020, 2021, 2022), each time linking science or standards to NCAP, so NCAP and its revision (NCAP 2.0) are must-study, along with source-sectors such as transport and waste.
focus: Sector-wise sources: transport, household fuels, waste, stubble

potential: "India's air pollution crisis is less a problem of knowledge than of implementation." Discuss. (15 marks)
Why have technological fixes such as smog towers failed to address air pollution? Suggest a more effective approach. (10 marks)
Examine how air pollution affects vulnerable sections disproportionately. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India's air pollution crisis is less a problem of knowledge than of implementation." Discuss.
parts: Why it is a problem of implementation

answer.t: The sources of India's air pollution, from transport and household fuels to waste and stubble burning, are well established, yet unhealthy air persists across the country all year round.

answer.h: Why it is a problem of implementation

pts.t: Sources are mapped, but cleaner transport, fuels and waste systems lag.
pts.ex: Year-round emissions from transport, waste burning and construction.

pts.t: Funds flow to visible gadgets of doubtful effect.
pts.ex: Smog towers and artificial rain.

pts.t: Pollution control boards are short of staff and powers.
pts.ex: Patchy enforcement on industry and construction dust.

pts.t: Airsheds cross state boundaries, but action is state-bound.
pts.ex: Stubble burning in Punjab, smog in Delhi.

pts.t: Rankings reward spending and plans, not cleaner air.
pts.ex: Critique of clean-air rankings (Oct 2026).

pts.t: Reform hits powerful lobbies in transport, industry and energy.
pts.ex: Resistance to stricter industrial norms.

pts.t: Ambient monitors miss what people breathe indoors and at work.
pts.ex: Women cooking on solid fuels.

pts.t: Monitoring is thin outside metros.
pts.ex: Air pollution is all-India, not only Delhi-NCR.

pts.t: Farmers' and households' choices are under-studied.
pts.ex: Economic constraints behind stubble burning.

pts.t: Secondary pollutant formation remains uncertain.
pts.ex: Winter smog episodes.

pts.t: Public transport, clean cooking, waste management and industrial regulation.
pts.ex: 'Moving people, not vehicles' (National Urban Transport Policy).

pts.t: Measure success by reduced exposure, with deadlines and accountability.
pts.ex: NCAP 2.0.

pts.t: Regional bodies with powers across states.
pts.ex: Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR.

pts.t: Make alternatives to burning economically viable.
pts.ex: Crop residue management machines, diversification.

pts.t: Safer workplaces and clean fuels for the poorest.
pts.ex: Clean cooking access for poor households.

pts.t: Independent evaluation of costly interventions.
pts.ex: Civil society questioning smog tower spending.

answer.t: India does not need to know everything to act on what it already knows; clean air depends on institutions, not gadgets.

title: 2-child norm for panchayat polls: Why SC says it's time for a rethink
syllabus: GS2 › Devolution of powers to local levels; local self-government · GS2 › Fundamental rights; judiciary · GS1 › Population; role of women · GS4 › Inclusive governance
summary: Explainer on the Supreme Court's referral of Javed v. State of Haryana (2003) to a larger Bench: with TFR at 1.9, the fear of overpopulation behind two-child rules for panchayat polls 'has crumbled'.
evolution: SC refers its 2003 ruling to a larger Bench (first card on the two-child norm).
Explained: the legal framework, Javed (2003) and what the court said now.
ideas: Two-child bar on panchayat office upheld in Javed (2003).
GS2 · Local government
Contesting is a statutory right.
TFR now 1.9, below replacement: the law's basis has gone.
GS1 · Population
Laws must change when facts change.
In a patriarchy it shuts women out of panchayats.
GS1 · Women / GS4 · Inclusive governance
Neutral law, unequal effect.
keywords: TFR of about 2.1, at which a population replaces itself
India's TFR of 1.9 is below replacement level, turning the population debate on its head.
A right created by law vs one guaranteed by the Constitution
Because contesting is a statutory right, legislatures can attach conditions, but they must still be reasonable.
data: India's total fertility rate when Javed was decided and now (replacement level: 2.1)
Supreme Court Bench, as reported
GS1 · Population
India's fertility rate has fallen from 3.0 in 2003 to 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1.

GS4
GS2 · Local democracy · GS4 · Inclusion

pyqs: Women's reservation in local government and patriarchal politics.
'Demographic winter' — is the world heading there?
Challenges of demographic transition in India.

trend.t: Demography questions turned from population control (women's empowerment and population, 2019) to ageing and decline ('demographic winter', 2024; demographic transition, 2026). Local government questions keep returning to women's representation (2019, 2026).
trend.watch: Demographic transition was asked in 2024 and 2026, so laws built for a high-fertility India, like the two-child norm, are strong examples.

potential: "Laws built for a high-fertility India may now hurt grassroots democracy." Examine with reference to two-child norms for panchayat elections. (10 marks)

title: Gender struggles must forge solidarities, not exclusion

summary: A women's group has asked the Supreme Court to stop recognising trans women as 'females' in official documents; the author argues debate must treat transgender persons as equal rights-bearers, not as a threat to women.

trend.t: Gender questions broadened from women's empowerment (2019, 2024) to constitutional gender justice (2023) and, in 2026, the rights of transgender persons under the amended Transgender Persons Act.
trend.watch: Transgender rights were asked directly in 2026, and rights-in-conflict framing is UPSC's favoured pattern, so the recognition debate is high-yield.

title: Tamil Nadu tightens grip on women-led electronics manufacturing
syllabus: GS1 › Role of women; Population and migration · GS3 › Employment; Industrial policy (manufacturing) · GS2 › Welfare of vulnerable sections; best practices in governance · GS4 › Innovation in public service; gender justice
summary: Annual Survey of Industries data for 2024-25 show Tamil Nadu employs 40.3% of all directly employed women factory workers in India and 44.4% of those making computer, electronic and optical products, helped by dormitories near factories.
evolution: Govt to study hurdles faced by women-led informal businesses (women and work thread).
Physicists bring STEM to women and rural youth.
ideas: Concentration of women's factory work: Tamil Nadu's share of directly employed women making computer, electronic and optical products rose from 42.9% to 44.4% in 2024-25; it employs 40.3% of all directly employed women factory workers in India.
GS1 · Women and work / GS3 · Manufacturing
Tamil Nadu employs two in five of India's directly employed women factory workers: proof that state policy shapes women's work.

A policy innovation that removes the real barriers: the two key obstacles for women are distance from work and living arrangements, and Tamil Nadu adapted China's model of dormitories for women workers.
GS4 · Innovation in public service / GS2 · Best practices
Tamil Nadu's factory dormitories are an innovation that solves women's real constraints, safety and distance, rather than offering only jobs.

Migration and an ageing south: southern states with ageing populations rely on migrant workers, so housing near factories is a key policy intervention; most surveyed migrants in the Chennai region came from Bihar, Odisha, Assam, UP and Jharkhand.
GS1 · Migration and demography
As the south ages and draws migrant workers from the east, worker housing becomes core industrial infrastructure.

A wide gender gap remains: directly employed women factory workers rose by 96,907 to 17.38 lakh, while men rose by 4.54 lakh to 78.78 lakh; Gujarat's share of women in electronics fell from 10% to 7.4%.
GS1 · Gender gap / GS3 · Employment
Women remain a small minority of India's factory workforce, so gains in one state must spread nationally.
A blind spot in the data: the survey gives no gender break-up of 70.31 lakh contract workers, so the true number of women in factories cannot be known.
GS3 · Employment data / GS2 · Statistics
Without gender data on contract workers, policy for women in factories is made half-blind.
keywords: Housing, transport, safety and childcare that let women take up jobs
Enabling infrastructure, not just job creation, decides whether women join the factory workforce.
Adapting a policy that worked elsewhere to local conditions
Tamil Nadu's dormitory model is policy transfer done well: borrowing the idea, adapting it to local needs.
Rising share of women in factory work, as in East Asian electronics
Electronics assembly can drive the feminisation of Indian manufacturing, as it did in East Asia.
Statistics broken down by sex to show gaps
Gender-disaggregated data on contract workers is the first step to gender-responsive labour policy.
Growing use of contract rather than directly employed workers
Contractualisation hides women workers from the statistics and from labour protections.

Urban migration of skilled, young, unmarried women and their freedom and family ties.
Continued challenges for women in India against time and space.
How patriarchy affects the middle-class working woman.

trend.t: Women questions moved from patriarchy and the working woman (2014) and globalisation's effects (2015) to challenges of 'time and space' (2019), the gig economy (2021), the care economy (2023) and gender concerns in programme design and women's migration (2024).
trend.watch: Women and work have been asked almost every year, so this is a must-study area. Questions now ask about the conditions that shape women's work, such as space, safety, care and migration, more than about the jobs themselves.
focus: Barriers to women's work: safety, mobility, care, housing
Women in manufacturing and services; migration

answer.t: The Annual Survey of Industries 2024-25 shows Tamil Nadu employs 40.3% of India's directly employed women factory workers, helped by dormitories that address distance and housing.

pts.ex: Tamil Nadu's dormitory model adapted from China.

pts.t: Safe housing and transport reassure women and their families.
Less commuting frees time and money.

pts.ex: Migrant workers in the Chennai region from Bihar, Odisha, Assam, UP and Jharkhand.

pts.ex: Tamil Nadu's 44.4% share of women in electronics manufacturing.

pts.t: Solving women's real constraints rather than only offering incentives is innovation in public service.

pts.ex: 70.31 lakh contract workers without gender data.

pts.t: Limited technical training restricts women to low-skill roles.
Strict rules can curb personal freedom.
Gains concentrate in a few states.
pts.ex: Gujarat's share fell from 10% to 7.4%.

pts.t: Industry-government partnerships for women's hostels near clusters.
pts.ex: Working women hostels announced in Budget 2024-25.

Night shifts with consent and safety, equal pay and grievance redress.
Train women for higher-skill electronics roles.
Gender break-up of contract workers in the ASI.
pts.ex: VISTAR statistics scheme (2026).

pts.t: Let other states adopt Tamil Nadu's model.

answer.t: Jobs open the factory door, but housing, safety and care let women walk through it; Tamil Nadu shows that a simple idea can turn women's potential into India's manufacturing strength.

title: More young women adopting menstrual hygiene
where: Your Health, page 12 (Policy Matters: Pally Kundu & Reena Singh, MoHFW)
syllabus: GS2 › Health; Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections and their performance · GS1 › Role of women; Social empowerment · GS4 › Dignity and compassion
summary: NFHS-6 shows 79.2% of women aged 15–24 use hygienic menstrual protection, up from 57.6% in 2015-16, the result of a multi-pronged government strategy.
ideas: A quiet social revolution: hygienic menstrual protection among women aged 15–24 has risen by about 22 percentage points since NFHS-4, so most young women have now moved off cloth and unsafe materials.
GS1 · Women / GS2 · Health
The rise in menstrual hygiene is an underrated marker of women's empowerment and public health progress.

Dignity is part of the definition: WHO–UNICEF define menstrual hygiene as clean material, changed in privacy, safely disposed of, without embarrassment or restriction, linking it to the SDGs on health and gender equality.
GS2 · Health / GS4 · Dignity
Menstrual hygiene is about dignity and freedom from restriction, not just products.

Multi-pronged delivery: the Scheme for Promotion of Menstrual Hygiene under the National Health Mission combines awareness for adolescent girls, subsidised napkins through ASHAs via schools and communities, and safe disposal.
GS2 · Welfare scheme design
Combining awareness, access and disposal through ASHAs and schools shows convergent scheme design.
Affordability through Jan Aushadhi: Suvidha sanitary pads at ₹1 each are distributed through Jan Aushadhi Kendras nationwide.
GS2 · Health access / Affordability
Pricing essential hygiene products at ₹1 removes cost as a barrier for poor households.
Beyond numbers: even small gains mean lakhs of young women switching to safe methods, part of a wider shift in how young women learn, decide and are heard.
GS1 · Social empowerment
Health gains among young women reinforce their education, agency and voice.
keywords: WHO–UNICEF standard of safe, private, dignified menstrual care
India tracks menstrual hygiene management against the WHO–UNICEF benchmark.
Several schemes and institutions working together
Menstrual hygiene gains show convergence of health, education and community platforms.
Services reaching households through ASHAs and schools
ASHAs show frontline delivery is the backbone of health outcomes.
data: Women aged 15–24 using hygienic menstrual protection; 77.6% in NFHS-5 (2019-21), 57.6% in NFHS-4 (2015-16)
NFHS-6, via IE
GS2 · Health / GS1 · Women
79.2% of young women now use hygienic menstrual protection, up from 57.6% in 2015-16 (NFHS-6).
100 crore+ / ₹1
Jan Aushadhi Suvidha sanitary pads sold by January 2026, priced at ₹1 per pad
